aboutAuthor: Kris Gopalakrishnan is a co-founder of Infosys and former CEO. N. Dayasindhu and Krishnan Narayanan are technology historians at ITiHAASA. Together they document the six-decade history of India's IT revolution through hundreds of interviews with industry pioneers.

points.heading: Software escaped the License Raj but needed shepherds
points.body: The invisibility of code helped it dodge the Kafkaesque controls that strangled hardware, yet the book shows that quiet statecraft from officials like N. Vittal and industry coordination via NASSCOM, not just benign neglect, turned avoidance into advantage.

points.heading: Hardware's fifty-machine cap shows policy without scale fails
points.body: A 1973 report to license minicomputers took five years and then capped each firm at fifty units a year, making viability impossible. The illustration of break-even volumes proves how anti-monopoly intent became an unviability guarantee.

points.heading: Mission-mode demand built capability before exports
points.body: NICNET's satellite network and the Railways' PRS reservation system gave Indian engineers demanding domestic customers. Those flowcharts and concurrency challenges later mapped directly to global banking and telecom reliability.

points.heading: STPI turned a garage into a global delivery node
points.body: The 1991 Software Technology Parks scheme, diagrammed as a 64 kbps earth station bypassing VSNL, eliminated the telecom bottleneck. Even a small office could become a bonded export zone, enabling the offshore model.

points.heading: Y2K was a reputational gateway more than a windfall
points.body: A 300 to 600 billion dollar global fix effort let Indian firms enter Fortune 500 data centers via low-risk date conversions, then stay for core systems. Revenue mattered less than the trust transfer that followed.

points.heading: Coming of age means knowledge arbitrage, not labor arbitrage
points.body: By 2019, 1,250 firms ran 1,750 capability centers, and labs like Cisco's ASR 901 team in Bengaluru showed R&D moving from support to ownership. The founder-tree to unicorns links services apprenticeships to product creation.

insights: N. Vittal's Birbal bargain: promise fourfold export growth in five years, then build STPI to make delivery possible.
The bullock-cart IBM 1620 at IIT Kanpur symbolizes how improvisation seeded a million-engineers-a-year pipeline.
Cutting bank onboarding from Rs 1,500 to Rs 10 via JAM shows how India Stack compresses inclusion costs by an order of magnitude.
conclusion: Against All Odds reframes a celebrated escape story as a co-built ascent: entrepreneurs supplied grit, educators supplied talent, and a handful of officials supplied the missing infrastructure. The pandemic epilogue proves the model could even leap from campuses to living rooms without breaking trust.
